summary_grc: ὁ Ἀριστοτέλης γράφει πῶς οἱ Ἀθηναῖοι τοὺς δικαστὰς κληρωτηρίοις ἐκλήρουν.
summary_en: Fourth-century Athens: how the jurors were chosen each morning by the allotment machine, and sent by a coloured staff to a court no one could predict. Aristotle's own words, lightly cut.
caption_grc: ἵν’ εἰς οἷον ἂν λάχῃ εἰσίῃ καὶ μὴ εἰς οἷον ἂν βούληται.

original.note: Aristotle (or a pupil), Constitution of the Athenians 63.4, 64.4 and 65.2, lightly cut; written about 330 BC, describing the courts of his own day, long after our story. The steps in between (64.1–3) are summarized in the second paragraph: the papyrus is damaged there. In the original, χρῶματα is printed for χρώματα.

grammar.md:
**Reading a procedure.** Aristotle describes what happens *every* court day, so he writes in the present and uses the constructions of repeated action (Units 8 and 10).

**1. General clauses: ἄν + subjunctive.** Any relative or temporal word + ἄν + subjunctive, with a present main verb, means 'whenever, wherever, whoever':

| clause | meaning |
|---|---|
| ἐπειδὰν ἴδῃ | whenever / as soon as he sees |
| ὅπου ἂν ᾖ ἐπιγεγραμμένον | wherever (in whichever box) there is written |
| εἰς οἷον ἂν λάχῃ | into whichever (court) he draws |
| οὓς ἂν βούληταί τις | whomever anyone wants |

ἐπειδάν = ἐπειδή + ἄν. For a single event in the past Greek uses the indicative without ἄν: ἐπειδὴ εἶδε 'when he saw'.

**2. The perfect passive: a state.** The perfect says that something done is still in force: ἐπιγέγραπται 'has been written on, is inscribed'; πινάκιον ἐπιγεγραμμένον τὸ ὄνομα 'a ticket inscribed with the name' (the passive participle can keep an accusative of the thing written); νενέμηνται 'they have been divided (and stay so)'. Look for reduplication (γέ-γραπ-ται, νε-νέμη-νται) and endings without a thematic vowel (-ται, -νται, -μένος).

**3. Article + participles.** ὁ κληθεὶς καὶ ὑπακούσας 'the man who has been called and has answered'; ὁ λαβὼν τὴν βακτηρίαν 'the man who has taken the staff'; παρὰ τοῦ εἰληχότος 'from the one who has drawn (the office)'. Aristotle names each person in the procedure by what he has just done.

**4. Likeness takes the dative.** ὁμόχρων τῇ βακτηρίᾳ 'the same colour as the staff', like ὁ αὐτὸς ἐκείνῳ, ὅμοιος τούτῳ.

culture.title: The kleroterion
culture.md:
Each year 6,000 citizens over thirty were enrolled as jurors and swore the jurors' oath. On a court day those who wanted to serve came to the entrances of the courts, tribe by tribe, and handed in their tickets. The **kleroterion** was a tall slab of stone with five columns of narrow slots, one column for each section letter, and a bronze tube down the side. The tickets were pushed into the slots; the archon poured a mixture of white and black balls into the tube and released them one at a time. A white ball selected a whole row of tickets, five jurors at once; a black one sent the row home. Then each chosen juror drew an acorn-token with a letter that sent him to a court, where he received a staff of the court's colour and, on entering, a token that he would exchange for his pay.

The point of all this machinery was to make bribery impossible: no one, not even the juror, knew in the morning which case he would hear, and a court had hundreds of jurors, 201, 501 or more. Fragments of several kleroteria and many bronze tickets have been found in the Athenian Agora; the picture shows one of them. A version of the same machine chose the members of the Council and most of the city's magistrates.
